source_text: Τοιοῦτος ἦν ὁ μακάριος Παῦλος· διὰ τοῦτο ἔλεγε· Τίς ἡμᾶς χωρίσει ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγάπης τοῦ Χριστοῦ; θλῖψις, ἢ στενοχωρία, ἢ διωγμὸς, ἢ λιμὸς, ἢ γυμνότης, ἢ κίνδυνος, ἢ μάχαιρα; καθὼς γέγραπται, ὅτι ἕνεκεν σοῦ θανατούμεθα ὅλην τὴν ἡμέραν, ἐλογίσθημεν ὡς πρόβατα σφαγῆς· ἀλλ' ἐν τούτοις πᾶσιν ὑπερνικῶμεν διὰ τοῦ ἀγαπήσαντος ἡμᾶς. Τοῦτο δὴ καὶ ἐνταῦθα αἰνιττόμενος ἔλεγεν, ὅτι Εἰ καὶ ὁ ἔξω ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος διαφθείρεται, ἀλλ' ὁ ἔσω ἀνακαινοῦται ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ· ἀσθενέστερον τὸ σῶμα γίνεται, φησὶν, ἀλλὰ δυνατωτέρα ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ ἰσχυροτέρα, καὶ πτεροῦται μᾶλλον. Καὶ καθάπερ στρατιώτης βαρύνοντα μὲν ἔχων ὅπλα, κἂν σφόδρα γενναῖος ᾖ καὶ πολεμικὸς, οὐκ ἂν γένοιτο τοῖς πολεμίοις φοβερὸς, τῆς τῶν ὅπλων βαρύτητος τῇ τῶν ποδῶν ταχύτητι καὶ τῇ τῶν πολεμικῶν ἐμπειρίᾳ λυμαινομένης· εἰ δὲ κοῦφα λάβοι καὶ εὐμεταχείριστα, πτηνοῦ παντὸς δίκην ἐπέρχεται τοῖς ἐναντίοις· οὕτω καὶ ὁ τὴν σάρκα τὴν ἑαυτοῦ μὴ μέθῃ, μηδὲ ἀνέσει καὶ τρυφῇ καταλιπαίνων, ἀλλὰ νηστείαις καὶ εὐχαῖς, καὶ τῇ πολλῇ τῶν θλίψεων ὑπομονῇ κουφοτέραν καὶ λεπτοτέραν κατασκευάζων, καθάπερ τις ὑπόπτερος ἄνωθεν καταβαίνων, οὕτω μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς ῥύμης εἰς τὰς τῶν δαιμόνων ἐμπίπτων φάλαγγας, καταφέρει ῥᾳδίως τὰς ἀντικειμένας δυνάμεις, καὶ ὑποχειρίους ποιεῖ. Οὕτω καὶ ὁ Παῦλος λαβὼν πολλὰς πληγὰς, καὶ εἰς τὸ δεσμωτήριον ἐμπεσὼν, καὶ ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ δεθεὶς, τὸ μὲν σῶμα ἀσθενέστερον εἶχε πόνοις κατατεινόμενον, τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν ἰσχυρὰν καὶ εὔτονον· καὶ οὕτως ἦν ἰσχυρὸς ὁ δεδεμένος, ὡς διὰ φωνῆς μόνης σαλεῦσαι τὰ θεμέλια τοῦ δεσμωτηρίου, καὶ τὸν λελυμένον δεσμοφύλακα δέσμιον εἰς τοὺς πόδας ἀγαγεῖν τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ, καὶ τὰς θύρας ἀποκεκλεισμένας ἀνοῖξαι. Οὐ μικρὰν οὖν ἡμῖν παραμυθίαν ἔδωκεν ὁ Παῦλος ταύτην καὶ πρὸ τῆς ἀναστάσεως, τὸ βελτίους ἡμᾶς γίνεσθαι καὶ φιλοσοφωτέρους τοῖς πειρασμοῖς. Διὰ τοῦτό φησιν· Ἡ θλῖψις ὑπομονὴν κατεργάζεται, ἡ δὲ ὑπομονὴ δοκιμὴν, ἡ δὲ δοκιμὴ ἐλπίδα, ἡ δὲ ἐλπὶς οὐ καταισχύνει Καὶ πάλιν ἄλλος τίς φησιν· Ἀνὴρ ἀπείραστος ἀδόκιμος, ὁ δὲ ἀδόκιμος οὐδενὸς ἄξιος λόγου. Ὥστε οὐ μικρὰ ἀπὸ τῆς θλίψεως καρπούμεθα καὶ πρὸ τῆς ἀναστάσεως, τὸ τὴν ψυχὴν ἔχειν δοκιμωτέραν καὶ σοφωτέραν καὶ συνετωτέραν, καὶ πάσης ἀπηλλάχθαι δειλίας. Διὰ τοῦτό φησιν· Εἰ καὶ ὁ ἔξω ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος διαφθείρεται, ἀλλ' ὁ ἔσω ἀνακαινοῦται ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ. Πῶς ἀνακαινοῦται, εἰπέ; Ἀνανδρίας ἐξελαυνομένης ἁπάσης, ἐπιθυμίας σβεννυμένης ἀτόπου, φιλοχρηματίας, κενοδοξίας, τῶν ἄλλων ἁπλῶς τῶν διεφθαρμένων λογισμῶν ἀναιρουμένων ἁπάντων. Ὥσπερ οὖν ἡ ἀργίας καὶ ἀδείας ἀπολαύουσα ψυχὴ εὐκόλως ὑπὸ τῶν παθῶν ἁλίσκεται τούτων· οὕτως ἡ διηνεκῶς τοῖς ἀγῶσι τοῖς ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐσεβείας ἐσχολακυῖα, οὐδὲ σχολὴν ἄγει ταῦτα ἐννοῆσαί ποτε, τῆς περὶ τὰ παλαίσματα μερίμνης πάντων αὐτὴν ἀπαγούσης ἐκείνων. Διὰ τοῦτο ἔλεγεν· Ἀνακαινοῦται ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ. Εἶτα πάλιν παραμυθούμενος τὰς ψυχὰς τὰς ὀδυνωμένας ἐπὶ τοῖς δεινοῖς τοῖς ἐπαγομένοις, καὶ οὐκ εἰδυίας φιλοσοφεῖν, διὰ τῆς ἐλπίδος τῶν μελλόντων αὐτὰς ἀνίστησιν, οὕτω λέγων· Τὸ γὰρ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως, καθ' ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολὴν αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης κατεργάζεται ἡμῖν, μὴ σκοπούντων ἡμῶν τὰ βλεπόμενα, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα.
thought_title: Paul as the blessed example of the soul made light by affliction
orientation: Chrysostom has just described the invulnerable soul and now presents Paul as its supreme example, quoting Romans 8 and 2 Corinthians 4 to show how affliction renews the inner self.
pass_a_gloss: Such was the blessed Paul; therefore he said: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? as it is written, that for your sake we are put to death all the day, we were counted as sheep of slaughter; but in all these things we are more than conquerors through the one who loved us. This indeed also here hinting at he said, that Even if our outer self is being corrupted, yet the inner self is being renewed day by day; the body becomes weaker, he says, but the soul more powerful and stronger, and is winged more. And just as a soldier having heavy weapons, even if he is very brave and warlike, would not become fearsome to the enemies, the heaviness of the weapons harming the swiftness of the feet and the experience in war; but if he takes light and easily handled weapons, in the manner of every winged thing he comes upon the opponents; so also the one who does not fatten his own flesh with drunkenness, nor with indulgence and luxury, but with fasts and prayers, and with much endurance of afflictions makes it lighter and finer, just as some winged one descending from above, so with much force falling upon the phalanxes of demons, he easily brings down the opposing powers, and makes them subject. So also Paul, having received many blows, and having fallen into the prison, and having been bound in the stocks, had the body weaker, strained by labors, but the soul strong and vigorous; and so strong was the bound man, that by voice alone he shook the foundations of the prison, and brought the released jailer as a prisoner to his own feet, and opened the doors that had been shut. Not small therefore consolation did Paul give us, this also before the resurrection, that we become better and more philosophical by trials. Therefore he says: Affliction produces endurance, and endurance produces testedness, and testedness produces hope, and hope does not put to shame. And again another someone says: An untested man is unapproved, and the unapproved man is worthy of no account. So that not small things do we harvest from affliction even before the resurrection, the having the soul more tested and wiser and more understanding, and freed from all cowardice. Therefore he says: Even if our outer self is being corrupted, yet the inner self is being renewed day by day. How is it renewed, tell me? All unmanliness being driven out, improper desire being quenched, love of money, vainglory, simply all the other corrupted thoughts being destroyed. Just as therefore the soul enjoying idleness and security is easily caught by these passions; so the soul continually occupied with the contests on behalf of piety does not even have leisure ever to think of these things, the concern about the wrestling matches drawing it away from all those things. Therefore he said: It is renewed day by day. Then again consoling the souls grieving over the terrible things brought upon them, and not knowing how to be philosophical, through the hope of the things to come he raises them up, saying thus: For the momentary lightness of affliction, beyond measure unto excess, an eternal weight of glory works for us, we not looking at the things seen, but at the things not seen.

choices.term: ὁ δὲ ἀδόκιμος οὐδενὸς ἄξιος λόγου
choices.english: and the unapproved man is worthy of no account
choices.why: ἀδόκιμος means 'unapproved, failing the test,' not 'rejected'; it pairs with ἀπείραστος ('untested') to describe someone who has not been proven by trial.
δοκιμή is the state of having been tested and approved; 'testedness' preserves the noun form and the link to δόκιμος/ἀδόκιμος.
The passive verb πτερόω means 'to be furnished with wings'; keeping it passive and literal preserves the image of the soul gaining wings through affliction.
The compound ὑπερνικάω intensifies νικάω; 'more than conquerors' is the standard rendering and captures the excess of victory.
The doubled phrase intensifies the degree; rendering both instances literally preserves the rhetorical force of the excess.
rejected: in a surpassing way to a surpassing degree

choices.why: ἀπείραστος means 'untried, untested,' and ἀδόκιμος means 'not standing the test, unapproved'; the pair describes lack of trial and lack of approval.

pass_b_english: Such was the blessed Paul. That is why he said: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? As it is written, ‘For your sake we are being killed all day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.’ But in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:35-37). This is what he was hinting at here when he said: “Even if our outer self is wasting away, yet the inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). The body becomes weaker, he says, but the soul becomes more powerful and stronger, and is winged more. Just as a soldier carrying heavy weapons, even if he is very brave and skilled in war, cannot be terrifying to his enemies, because the weight of his weapons undermines the speed of his feet and his experience in battle—but if he takes light and easily handled weapons, he comes upon his opponents like any winged creature—so also the one who does not fatten his own flesh with drunkenness or with ease and luxury, but makes it lighter and thinner through fasts and prayers and great endurance of afflictions, descends from above like a winged being, and with great force falls upon the phalanxes of demons, easily overthrows the opposing powers, and makes them subject to him. So Paul, after receiving many blows and being thrown into prison and bound in the stocks, had a body made weaker by being stretched with labors, but a soul strong and vigorous. And the bound man was so strong that by his voice alone he shook the foundations of the prison, brought the unbound jailer bound to his own feet, and opened the doors that had been shut. Paul therefore gave us no small comfort even before the resurrection: that we become better and more philosophical through trials. That is why he says: “Affliction produces endurance, and endurance produces testedness, and testedness produces hope, and hope does not put to shame” (Romans 5:3-5). And again someone else says: “An untested man is unapproved, and the unapproved man is worthy of no account.” So we reap no small fruit from affliction even before the resurrection: having a soul that is more tested, wiser, and more understanding, and freed from all cowardice. That is why he says: “Even if our outer self is wasting away, yet the inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). How is it renewed? Tell me. All unmanliness is driven out, disordered desire is quenched, love of money, vainglory, and simply all the other corrupted thoughts are destroyed. Just as a soul enjoying idleness and security is easily captured by these passions, so the soul continually occupied with contests for godliness never has leisure even to think of them, since concern about its wrestling matches draws it away from all those things. That is why he said: “It is being renewed day by day.” Then again, comforting the souls that grieve over the terrible things that come upon them and do not know how to be philosophical, he raises them up through the hope of things to come, saying: “For this momentary light affliction is working out for us, beyond measure unto excess, an eternal weight of glory, while we look not at the things that are seen, but at the things that are not seen” (2 Corinthians 4:17-18).

last_rejected.why: κατατεινόμενον means worn down/consumed by pains, not 'stretched'. Misleads reader about Paul's condition.
last_rejected.ruling: κατατεινόμενον from κατατείνω means 'stretched'/'strained'; 'stretched with labors' is within normal semantic range, not misleading.

last_rejected.source_quote: Τίς ἡμᾶς χωρίσει ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγάπης τοῦ Χριστοῦ; θλῖψις, ἢ στενοχωρία, ἢ διωγμὸς, ἢ λιμὸς, ἢ γυμνότης, ἢ κίνδυνος, ἢ μάχαιρα; καθὼς γέγραπται, ὅτι ἕνεκεν σοῦ θανατούμεθα ὅλην τὴν ἡμέραν, ἐλογίσθημεν ὡς πρόβατα σφαγῆς· ἀλλ' ἐν τούτοις πᾶσιν ὑπερνικῶμεν διὰ τοῦ ἀγαπήσαντος ἡμᾶς
last_rejected.why: The quotation matches Romans 8:35-37, but Chrysostom attributes this to Paul without specifying Romans; more critically, the source shows this is introduced as Paul's own words (διὰ τοῦτο ἔλεγε), not as a formal scripture citation with book reference. The English adds a modern citation not in the source text.
last_rejected.fix: Remove '(Romans 8:35-37)' or place it in a footnote; the text simply says 'he said'.
last_rejected.ruling: Citation (Rom 8:35-37) is standard editorial reference; source quotes Paul's words accurately. Not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: And again someone else says: "An untested man is unapproved, and the unapproved man is worthy of no account."
last_rejected.source_quote: Καὶ πάλιν ἄλλος τίς φησιν· Ἀνὴρ ἀπείραστος ἀδόκιμος, ὁ δὲ ἀδόκιμος οὐδενὸς ἄξιος λόγου
last_rejected.why: The English 'someone else' obscures that this is a proverb/wise saying, not a named speaker. But more seriously, the English makes this sound like a separate quotation from an unidentified person, when Chrysostom presents it as a general truth, not a voice distinct from Paul's teaching.
last_rejected.fix: And again there is a saying: 'An untested man...'
last_rejected.ruling: ἄλλος τίς = 'someone else'; English correctly renders. No misleading change in meaning.

last_rejected.why: 'Philosophical' in modern English suggests theoretical speculation; Chrysostom means 'more devoted to wisdom/virtue, more self-controlled' in the ancient sense. The word's semantic range includes 'wise, temperate, virtuous'—'philosophical' misleads modern readers.
last_rejected.ruling: φιλοσοφώτερος includes 'philosophical' in patristic usage; within normal range, not a mistranslation.

last_rejected.quote: do not know how to be philosophical
last_rejected.why: Same problem: 'philosophical' is a false friend. Here φιλοσοφεῖν means 'to endure with wisdom/fortitude, to be resigned and wise in suffering,' not to engage in philosophy.
last_rejected.fix: do not know how to bear suffering with wisdom
last_rejected.ruling: φιλοσοφεῖν rendered 'be philosophical' is within normal range; not a meaning change or loss.

last_rejected.quote: he raises them up through the hope of things to come, saying:
last_rejected.source_quote: διὰ τῆς ἐλπίδος τῶν μελλόντων αὐτὰς ἀνίστησιν, οὕτω λέγων· Τὸ γὰρ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως
last_rejected.why: The English omits the crucial word παραυτίκα ('momentary, for the present') which contrasts with 'eternal.' This temporal contrast is central to Paul's argument and Chrysostom's consolation.
last_rejected.fix: he raises them up through the hope of things to come, saying: 'For the momentary lightness of affliction...'
last_rejected.ruling: παραυτίκα appears in the quoted scripture 'momentary light affliction'; not omitted, just in the citation.
